Imitating the Imperfect: Offline-to-Online Robust Imitation Learning from Heterogeneous Demonstrators

Cheng Pan Email: cheng.pan@epfl.ch Affiliation: Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne (EPFL), Lausanne, Switzerland    Nan Lu Email: nan.lu@bristol.ac.uk Affiliation: University of Bristol, Bristol, UK    Kai Arulkumaran Email: kailash@sakana.ai Affiliation: Araya Inc., Tokyo, Japan    Josie Hughes Email: josie.hughes@epfl.ch Affiliation: Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne (EPFL), Lausanne, Switzerland
Abstract

Imitation learning (IL) typically relies on large-scale offline demonstrations collected from multiple human or algorithmic demonstrators. However, most existing approaches assume these demonstrators are homogeneous or near-optimal experts, a convenient but unrealistic assumption in real-world applications. In practice, demonstrations are often collected from heterogeneous demonstrators with unknown and varying levels of expertise, resulting in highly mixed-quality data. In this work, we study a challenging yet practical setting of imitation learning from such heterogeneous imperfect demonstrators. We propose Latent Expertise and Optimality Scoring based Imitation Learning (LEOS-IL), a principled framework that jointly learns (i) a state-action optimality scoring model and (ii) latent expertise levels for each demonstrator from unlabeled suboptimal offline demonstrations. The learned scoring model is then integrated into an online policy optimization procedure, where the agent is trained to maximize estimated optimality scores while its online rollouts are iteratively leveraged to refine the scoring model, thereby mitigating distributional shift during online adaptation. We further provide theoretical guarantees for optimality score identification and conditional optimal occupancy and policy recovery under explicit sufficient conditions. Experiments on continuous control benchmarks demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms existing baselines across highly heterogeneous and low-quality demonstration regimes.

keywords
Imitation Learning, Heterogeneous Demonstrators, Optimality Estimation, Unknown Expertise, Offline-to-Online

1 Introduction

Imitation learning (IL) offers a convenient framework that enables agents to acquire skills directly from expert demonstrations Zare et al. (2024). Prior research has shown that effective policies can be learned efficiently when provided with large-scale and high-quality demonstrations Belkhale et al. (2023); Saxena et al. (2025). However, in real-world scenarios, large-scale datasets are often collected from multiple demonstrators, and human or algorithmic demonstrators typically possess strengths in specific contexts and may perform suboptimally outside their areas of expertise. For example, in autonomous driving data collected from electric vehicles Lee et al. (2022); Zhang et al. (2024), drivers demonstrate a wide range of skill levels, resulting in heterogeneous and imperfect trajectories with unknown degrees of expertise. Treating all such demonstrators as perfect experts can lead to unreliable or even unsafe agent behavior, posing serious risks in safety-critical applications.

In this work, we study IL from heterogeneous imperfect demonstrators whose expertise levels are unknown and variable, naturally leading to datasets containing suboptimal demonstrations, and learn a policy online based on the estimated demonstrator expertise and data optimality. Existing methods (see details in Section 2) addressing this setting often rely on one or more of the following assumptions: (i) demonstrators are homogeneous, i.e., with the same expertise levels, and the optimal data dominates the dataset, (ii) access to explicit labels indicating the optimality of demonstrations, or (iii) the expertise level of each demonstrator is known a priori. These requirements are demanding and often impractical when demonstrations come from uncontrolled or large-scale sources.

This brings us to a central question: Can we design effective IL algorithms without relying on these assumptions? This problem setting is inherently challenging because neither demonstrator expertise levels nor demonstration optimality are observed. In the worst case, all demonstrators may exhibit very low expertise, making it extremely difficult to extract reliable signals for policy learning.

To address the challenges, we propose a novel Latent Expertise and Optimality Scoring based Imitation Learning framework (LEOS-IL) for learning from heterogeneous imperfect demonstrators. Our main contributions are summarized below.

Contribution 1: A formulation for modeling heterogeneous imperfect demonstrators.

We introduce a principled formulation in which each demonstrator is modeled as a flexible mixture of optimal and suboptimal behaviors. We characterize a demonstrator’s expertise level as the probability of selecting actions aligned with an underlying latent optimal policy. These expertise levels vary across demonstrators, naturally capturing heterogeneous demonstration quality, while remaining fully latent and unobserved. This formulation provides a principled foundation for learning from realistic mixed-quality datasets without requiring explicit supervision11 1 We only require 1 expert query to resolve ambiguity from the purely unsupervised setting (Sec. 3.2.2). or curated expert data.

Contribution 2: A principled offline-to-online heterogeneous IL framework.

Building on this formulation, we propose a novel two-stage IL framework (Fig. 1). In the offline stage (Stage 1), we jointly estimate demonstrator expertise and learn a scoring model that assigns optimality scores to each state-action pair, representing the likelihood that the pair corresponds to the (latent) optimal policy. This is achieved through an EM-style alternating self-training method that iteratively refines the scoring model and expertise estimates based on its current hard pseudo-labels. In the online stage (Stage 2), the learned scoring model is used as a surrogate reward function for policy optimization. To address the distributional shift arising from offline training, we introduce an online iterative refinement procedure that alternates between policy learning and scoring model fine-tuning, yielding a progressively less biased and more informative reward signal.

Contribution 3: Theoretical and empirical validation.

We provide theoretical analysis establishing optimality-score identification and conditional optimal occupancy and policy recovery under explicit sufficient conditions. Empirically, we evaluate our method in two challenging heterogeneous scenarios: (i) a wide-range setting, with demonstrator expertise levels spanning [0.1,0.9][0.1,0.9], and (ii) a low-quality setting, where all demonstrators are highly suboptimal with expertise in [0.05,0.15][0.05,0.15]. Across both regimes, our method outperforms baselines and, remarkably, achieves performance comparable to methods trained on the subset of purely optimal demonstrations. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework for learning from uncurated demonstrations with unknown and highly variable quality.

2 Related work

We review imitation learning methods under different assumptions on demonstration quality, demonstrator heterogeneity, and supervision. The comparison between our method and representative IL baselines is summarized in Table 1.

IL with Homogeneous Demonstrators

A large body of IL research assumes that demonstrations originate from a single, near-optimal expert policy. This assumption underpins classical approaches such as behavior cloning (Pomerleau, 1988, BC;), as well as more recent methods such as generative adversarial imitation learning (Ho and Ermon, 2016, GAIL;), which matches the state-action occupancy measures of the learner and the demonstrator via adversarial training. Methods designed to handle noisy demonstrations, such as robust imitation learning (Tangkaratt et al., 2020, RIL;), also implicitly retain this homogeneity assumption by modeling demonstrator behavior as arising from a mixture of optimal and suboptimal policies, with a single mixing coefficient representing the expertise level, and by assuming that expert data dominates the dataset. While effective under relatively homogeneous conditions, these methods may be less well suited to settings where demonstrator expertise varies widely.

IL with Optimality Labels

To better handle suboptimal demonstrations, many IL methods use supervision to distinguish optimal from non-optimal behavior. Extensions of GAIL, such as imperfect demonstration and confidence GAIL (Wu et al., 2019, IC-GAIL;) uses confidence labels to reweight imperfect demonstrations, whereas positive-unlabeled-style GAIL for unlabeled imperfect demonstrations (Wang et al., 2023, UID-GAIL;) does not assume labeled successful trajectories. Instead, it treats the demonstration set as an unlabeled mixture and uses a positive-unlabeled-style risk decomposition based on the current policy occupancy to guide learning toward the residual demonstration distribution. Similarly, example-based methods like recursive classification of examples (Eysenbach et al., 2021, RCE;) train success classifiers from labeled examples to create proxy rewards. These methods are effective when labeled data are available, but their applicability can be limited when such supervision is difficult to obtain.

IL from Heterogeneous and Imperfect Demonstrations

More recent efforts relax the assumption of homogeneous, near-optimal demonstrations. Weighted GAIL (Wang et al., 2021, WGAIL;) estimates importance weights from discriminator outputs to emphasize higher-quality samples without requiring known expertise levels. IL by estimating expertise of demonstrators (Beliaev et al., 2022, ILEED;) jointly estimates a policy and state-dependent demonstrator expertise through offline maximum likelihood, but models suboptimal behavior through uniform action selection and does not use environment interaction for subsequent refinement. Variational IL with diverse-quality demonstrations (Tangkaratt et al., 2020, VILD;) explicitly considers demonstrators of unknown and diverse quality and jointly infers expertise and reward, but explains heterogeneity through demonstrator-specific corruption of latent optimal actions. Other closely related methods obtain additional quality information through limited supervision. Learning to discern (Kuhar et al., 2023, L2D;) uses sparse quality annotations together with temporal representation learning to identify high-quality demonstrations across different behavioral styles, while preference aided IL from imperfect demonstrations (Cao et al., 2024, PAIL;) learns a reward from pairwise human preferences and uses it to reweight demonstrations and incorporate high-quality learner-generated trajectories. In contrast, our method instead primarily exploits heterogeneity across demonstrators as surrogate supervision and models expertise at two complementary levels: a demonstrator-level expertise parameter capturing overall skill and a state--action optimality posterior capturing context-specific quality. By combining this two-level expertise model with online scorer refinement, our framework turns heterogeneous, low-quality demonstrations into a usable learning signal for policy improvement with only minimal supervision.22 2 We provide further discussion and comparisons with related methods in Supplementary Sec. S1.

3 IL from heterogeneous demonstrators

In this section, we formally formulate the problem of IL from heterogeneous demonstrators and propose our method.

3.1 Problem Setup

In reinforcement learning (Sutton et al., 1998, RL;), the optimal policy maximizes the expected cumulative reward: π∗=arg⁡maxπ​𝔼pπ​[∑t=1Tγt​r​(st,at)],\pi^{*}=\arg\!\max_{\pi}\mathbb{E}_{p_{\pi}}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\gamma^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\right], where r⁡(st,at)r(s_{t},a_{t}) is the reward associated with the state-action pair (s,a)(s,a) at time tt, pπp_{\pi} is the trajectory distribution induced by policy π\pi, and γ\gamma is the discount factor. Unlike RL, in IL the reward function is unobserved and learning relies on a dataset of demonstrator trajectories τ={(s0,a0),…,(sTτ,aTτ)}\tau=\{(s_{0},a_{0}),...,(s_{T_{\tau}},a_{T_{\tau}})\} of varying lengths TτT_{\tau}. The goal is to learn a policy π\pi that matches the optimal policy’s state-action distribution.

To make this feasible, most IL algorithms assume that all demonstrations are generated by the optimal policy. However, this assumption is restrictive as real datasets are often collected from multiple demonstrators with varying skills. Therefore, in this work, we study IL from heterogeneous demonstrators with different and unknown expertise.

Dataset: We consider mm demonstrators. Each demonstrator i∈[m]i\in[m] provides a set of trajectories DiD_{i} and is associated with an expertise level αi∈[0,1]\alpha_{i}\in[0,1]. We define αi\alpha_{i} as the probability that any given (s,a)(s,a) pair from DiD_{i} was generated by the optimal policy, i.e., αi=ℙ⁡[(s,a)∼π∗|(s,a)∈Di]\alpha_{i}=\mathbb{P}[(s,a)\sim\pi^{*}|(s,a)\in D_{i}]. This represents a demonstrator-level attribute: a higher αi\alpha_{i} means demonstrator ii tends to act more consistently w.r.t. π∗\pi^{*}. We consider demonstrator heterogeneity, i.e., ∃i,j∈[m],i≠j\exists~i,j\in[m],i\neq j, such that αi≠αj\alpha_{i}\neq\alpha_{j}. The full dataset is D={(i,Di)}i=1mD=\{(i,D_{i})\}_{i=1}^{m}, and the expertise levels {αi}i=1m\{\alpha_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m} are unknown.

Optimality Score: For each (s,a)(s,a) pair, we introduce a binary latent variable z∈{0,1}z\in\{0,1\} indicating its optimality: z=1⇒(s,a)∼π∗z=1\Rightarrow(s,a)\sim\pi^{*}, while z=0⇒(s,a)∼πsubz=0\Rightarrow(s,a)\sim\pi^{\mathrm{sub}}, where πsub\pi^{\mathrm{sub}} denotes an unknown suboptimal policy. 3.2 Joint estimation of expertise and scoring model

We now describe how to learn the scoring model fϕf_{\phi} directly from the heterogeneous dataset DD.

3.2.1 Surrogate demonstrator classification for optimality scoring

The optimality scoring task can be framed as a binary class probability estimation Buja et al. (2005) problem, where we aim to estimate ℙ⁡(z=1|s,a)\mathbb{P}(z=1|s,a) for each (s,a)(s,a) pair being optimal (with label z=1z=1) or sub-optimal (with label z=0z=0). In the supervised setting, if explicit optimality labels zz were available, one could directly train fϕf_{\phi} with a proper scoring rule, such as cross-entropy. However, in our setting, such labels are not available. To address this challenge, we adapt the surrogate learning framework from the surrogate set classification (SSC) method of Lu et al. (2021).

Surrogate Demonstrator Classification

We use the demonstrator identity z¯∈[m]\bar{z}\in[m] as a surrogate label. Then the surrogate task involves training a multi-class classifier f¯ϕ:𝒮×𝒜→ℝm\overline{f}_{\phi}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}^{m} to predict the demonstrator from which each (s,a)(s,a) pair originated, by minimizing the risk:

where μi\mu_{i} is the empirical prior probability of sampling from demonstrator ii, estimated as μi:=|Di|∑i=1m|Di|\mu_{i}:=\frac{{|D_{i}|}}{\sum_{i=1}^{m}{|D_{i}|}}, where |Di||D_{i}| denotes the cardinality of the dataset DiD_{i}, and ℓ\ell is the cross-entropy loss. Lemma 1 (Optimal Scoring Model Recovery, Lu et al. (2021)).

Assume the model class is well-specified, ℓ\ell is a proper loss (e.g., cross-entropy), and TT is correctly computed as in Eq. 2. Let f¯ϕ\overline{f}_{\phi} be the surrogate classifier trained optimally according to Eq. 3. Then the induced binary scoring model fϕf_{\phi} accurately estimates the optimality scores: fϕ​(s,a)=ℙ⁡(z=1∣s,a)f_{\phi}(s,a)=\mathbb{P}(z=1\mid s,a).

An exact optimality scoring model identifies the optimal component of the demonstration distribution through a density-reweighting relation. We use rϕ​(s,a)=−log⁡(1−fϕ​(s,a))r_{\phi}(s,a)=-\log(1-f_{\phi}(s,a)) as the surrogate reward for policy learning. Although this transformation is monotonically increasing in the optimality posterior and therefore preserves the ordering of state–action pairs, maximizing it pointwise does not in general guarantee recovery of the full optimal occupancy. In particular, it may favor policies that concentrate occupancy on a subset of highly rewarded state–action pairs. We therefore distinguish optimality-score identification from policy recovery. The following theorem provides a sufficient condition under which maximizing the transformed surrogate reward recovers the optimal occupancy.

Theorem 2 (Conditional Optimal Occupancy Recovery).

Let π∗\pi^{\ast} be the unknown optimal policy and assume that π∗\pi^{\ast} belongs to the feasible learner policy class. Theorem 2 is deliberately conditional. Eq. 4 bounds the reward-weighted concentration of any feasible learner occupancy relative to the optimal-policy occupancy. It rules out policies that obtain a larger surrogate return simply by concentrating occupancy on a subset of high-reward state–action pairs.

3.2.2 EM-style alternating optimization of scoring model and expertise estimates

However, neither optimality labels nor expertise are given in our setting. To jointly learn both, we propose an EM-style alternating self-training method (Algorithm 1).66 6 To make the expertise level estimation problem solvable, we assume the existence of anchor points in the demonstration dataset, i.e., data points that belong to class z=1z=1 and z=0z=0 almost surely. Here, EM-style refers to the alternating updates of the scoring model and demonstrator expertise estimates.

The algorithm begins by randomly initializing the expertise levels {αi}i=1m\{\alpha_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m} within the range [0.1,0.9][0.1,0.9]. Given the initial {αi}i=1m\{\alpha_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}, we update the scoring model fϕf_{\phi} using the surrogate objective Eq. 3. We treat the expected expertise level α′\alpha^{\prime} of the target environment as a hyperparameter and fix it to 0.50.5. This choice corresponds to evaluating the scoring model using the balanced risk, a criterion adopted in Tangkaratt et al. (2020) and shown to be robust to label noise Charoenphakdee et al. (2019); Menon et al. (2015). We further justify this choice through ablation studies presented in Supplementary Tables S5–S6 and Supplementary Fig. S5. Next, the current scoring model produces hard pseudo-labels z^(s,a)={fϕ(s,a)>0.5}\hat{z}(s,a)=\mathbf{1}\!\left\{f_{\phi}(s,a)>0.5\right\}. Interpreting fϕ​(s,a)f_{\phi}(s,a) as the posterior probability ℙ⁡(z=1∣s,a)\mathbb{P}(z=1\mid s,a), this threshold corresponds to the Bayes-optimal classifier under symmetric 00–11 loss. We then estimate each αi\alpha_{i} as the empirical fraction of samples from demonstrator ii assigned z^=1\hat{z}=1. This alternating self-training procedure is repeated for TT epochs.

To reduce sensitivity to the initialization of {αi}i=1m\{\alpha_{i}\}^{m}_{i=1}, we run the algorithm with multiple random initializations until the Expertise Dispersion Criterion is satisfied. We report the number of initializations required in Supplementary Table S7.

Expertise Dispersion Criterion

Since our algorithm trains on self-labeled data, it is susceptible to error propagation and confirmation bias. In practice, some random initializations lead to degenerate solutions, where fϕ​(s,a)f_{\phi}(s,a) becomes overly confident and the estimated expertise levels collapse to nearly identical values. To assess the reliability of the learned expertise levels {αi}i=1m\{\alpha_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}, we measure their dispersion by computing the variance Var⁡({αi}i=1m)\mathrm{Var}(\{\alpha_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}). If the variance falls below a small threshold ϵ>0\epsilon>0, we consider the model to have failed in distinguishing between different expertise levels, yielding low-information, overfit predictions. Conversely, a higher variance suggests more informative and diverse estimates, suggesting the model has captured demonstrator heterogeneity. We therefore use this variance as a selection criterion to retain only solutions with sufficient dispersion in {αi}i=1m\{\alpha_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}. If Var⁡({αi}i=1m)<ϵ\mathrm{Var}(\{\alpha_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m})<\epsilon, we restart Algorithm 1 with a fresh random initialization; otherwise, we retain the learned model. We use ϵ=0.0005\epsilon=0.0005 in all experiments (all hyperparameters are given in Appendix Table 77).

Optimality Alignment Criterion

Due to the unsupervised nature of our setting, the learned scoring model may inadvertently invert the notion of optimality. In such cases, the estimated expertise levels αi\alpha_{i} may effectively correspond to 1−αi1-\alpha_{i}.

To detect and correct this issue, we query a small subset of state–action pairs and ask an expert to verify their predicted labels. We use five queries in the main experiments, while the ablation shows that a single query performs comparably (Supplementary Tables S3–S4 and Supplementary Fig. S4).

If the majority of results indicate a systematic inversion in predicted labels, we simply flip the predicted labels and correct the outputs as follows: αi←1−αi,fϕ​(s,a)←1−fϕ​(s,a),∀i∈[m],∀(s,a)∈D.\alpha_{i}\leftarrow 1-\alpha_{i},f_{\phi}(s,a)\leftarrow 1-f_{\phi}(s,a),\forall i\in[m],~\forall(s,a)\in D.

3.3 Imitation learning via scoring model

After learning the scoring model fϕf_{\phi} and estimating the expertise levels {α}i=1m\{\alpha\}_{i=1}^{m}, we perform IL.

3.3.1 Progressive scoring model refinement via fine-grained sample selection

The scoring model fϕf_{\phi} is initially trained only on demonstration data, limiting its generalization to learner trajectories due to covariate shift Chang et al. (2021). To improve its robustness, we refine fϕf_{\phi} during agent learning using three complementary terms: demonstration discriminative loss (Eq. 3), reflecting the original training signal; agent-matching penalty, discouraging the misclassification of learner-generated behaviors as optimal; and a mixup regularizer Zhang et al. (2017) which interpolates between agent and demonstrator behaviors to smooth the scoring boundary and stabilize training. The resulting objective is:

minϕ\displaystyle{\min_{\phi}}\ 𝔼^(s,a)∼ρ​[ℓ⁡(T⁡(fϕ​(s,a)),z¯)]+𝔼^(s′,a′)∼ρπθ​[−log⁡(1−fϕ​(s′,a′))]\displaystyle\widehat{\mathbb{E}}_{(s,a)\sim\rho}{\big[\ell(T(f_{\phi}(s,a)),\bar{z})\big]}+\widehat{\mathbb{E}}_{(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})\sim\rho^{\pi_{\theta}}}{\big[-\log(1-f_{\phi}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime}))\big]}
+wmix​𝔼^(s,a)∼ρ^π∗(s′,a′)∼ρπθ​[ℒmixup​(s,a,s′,a′)]\displaystyle+{w_{\mathrm{mix}}}\widehat{\mathbb{E}}_{\begin{subarray}{c}(s,a)\sim\hat{\rho}^{\pi^{*}}\\ (s^{\prime},a^{\prime})\sim\rho^{\pi_{\theta}}\end{subarray}}\big[\mathcal{L}_{\text{mixup}}(s,a,s^{\prime},a^{\prime})\big] (5)

where 𝔼^\widehat{\mathbb{E}} denotes empirical expectation; ρ^π∗\hat{\rho}^{\pi^{*}} represents pseudo-optimal data inferred from Dopt⊆DD_{\text{opt}}\subseteq D; and wmix>0w_{\mathrm{mix}}>0 denotes the mixup loss weight. We set wmix=2w_{\mathrm{mix}}=2 for all of our experiments. The mixup loss is

ℒmixup=−λ​log⁡(fϕ​(s~,a~))−(1−λ)​log⁡(1−fϕ​(s~,a~)),\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{mixup}}={-\lambda\log\!\big(f_{\phi}(\tilde{s},\tilde{a})\big)-(1-\lambda)\log\!\big(1-f_{\phi}(\tilde{s},\tilde{a})\big)},
where​(s~,a~)=λ⁡(s,a)+(1−λ)​(s′,a′),λ∼𝒰⁡(0,1)\displaystyle\text{where}\ {(\tilde{s},\tilde{a})=\lambda(s,a)+(1-\lambda)(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})},\quad\lambda\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1)

Early in training, the novice agent tends to produce suboptimal behaviors. The agent-matching penalty discourages fϕf_{\phi} from assigning high scores to these early samples, thereby enhancing its ability to distinguish between agent and demonstrator behavior and reducing covariate shift. In parallel, mixup acts as both data augmentation and regularization based on agent and expert data, yielding more stable and informative gradients, ultimately improving the effectiveness of policy learning in IL Orsini et al. (2021). The full training procedure is given in Algorithm 2.

To further refine fϕf_{\phi}, we adopt a bootstrapping approach where fϕf_{\phi} is used to pseudo-label demonstration data DD. At each iteration: (1) we extract a pseudo-optimal subset Dopt⊆DD_{\text{opt}}\subseteq D by applying a top-kk selection method, where we choose the ⌊k⋅|D|⌋\lfloor k\cdot|D|\rfloor state–action pairs with the highest fϕf_{\phi} scores (⌊⋅⌋\lfloor\cdot\rfloor denotes the floor function); (2) we generate new agent trajectories DπθD_{\pi_{\theta}} to represent ρπθ\rho^{\pi_{\theta}}\ ; (3) we update fϕf_{\phi} using the loss in Eq. 5 (Algorithm 2 Line 5), computed over DD, DπθD_{\pi_{\theta}}, and DoptD_{\text{opt}}; (4) we relabel DoptD_{\text{opt}} using the updated fϕf_{\phi} (Algorithm 2 Line 7). This mutual reinforcement between scoring model refinement and pseudo-label improvement allows both components to jointly bootstrap toward higher fidelity.

3.3.2 Policy learning with scoring model as a surrogate reward

As training progresses, the agent begins to generate increasingly competent behaviors, which are nonetheless treated as suboptimal during scoring model refinement. At this stage, the scoring model fϕf_{\phi} functions similarly to a discriminator in the GAIL framework Ho and Ermon (2016), struggling to distinguish between optimal and agent-generated data. Despite this, our approach is fundamentally different from GAIL, which relies exclusively on optimal demonstrations: our method operates in an (almost) unsupervised setting, allowing fϕf_{\phi} to learn from offline suboptimal data from heterogeneous demonstrators. This makes our approach especially effective when demonstration quality is low.

As the agent improves, fϕf_{\phi} becomes increasingly confused, and its predictions become unreliable. To prevent the accumulation of incorrect labels that could mislead policy learning, we introduce an early stopping criterion for the relabeling process: let Δt\Delta_{t} denote the number of sample changes in DoptD_{\text{opt}} between iterations tt and t−1t-1, counting both removed and newly added samples; if Δt<δ\Delta_{t}<\delta for pp consecutive steps, we stop relabeling and freeze DoptD_{\text{opt}}. The updated fϕf_{\phi} is employed as a surrogate reward function for training the agent policy πθ\pi_{\theta} (Algorithm 2 Line 10). Specifically, letting gϕ​(s,a)g_{\phi}(s,a) denote the scorer logit and fϕ​(s,a)=σ⁡(gϕ​(s,a))f_{\phi}(s,a)=\sigma(g_{\phi}(s,a)), we use the surrogate reward rϕ​(s,a)=−log⁡(1−fϕ​(s,a))=softplus⁡(gϕ​(s,a))r_{\phi}(s,a)=-\log(1-f_{\phi}(s,a))=\operatorname{softplus}(g_{\phi}(s,a)). In practice, we update the policy using soft actor-critic (Haarnoja et al., 2018, SAC;), alternating with scoring model refinement and pseudo-label updates.

4 Experiments

We test whether our algorithm can (1) train a scoring model on multiple sets of imperfect demonstration data collected from heterogeneous demonstrators in order to provide optimality labels and estimate demonstrator expertise levels, and (2) learn an optimal agent policy based on the scoring model and imperfect demonstrations.

To evaluate the robustness of our algorithm under widely varying and low demonstrator expertise, we design two experiments: (a) General expertise test, using demonstrations collected from varying expertise levels in a wide range [0.1−0.9][0.1-0.9] (average optimal ratio 0.5), and (b) Low expertise test, with extremely low expertise levels in [0.05−0.15][0.05-0.15] (average optimal ratio 0.1). Prior works mostly focused on cases where most demonstrations are optimal, with limited exploration of low-optimal-ratio settings, where their performance degrades significantly Eysenbach et al. (2021); Wang et al. (2021); Wang et al. (2023). To address this gap, we specifically evaluate the low expertise setting. In both tests, datasets are constructed from six demonstrators (each providing 5,000 samples) with uniformly distributed expertise levels (see Appendix Table 72). We set the top-kk hyperparameter kk to match the average optimal ratio in each test. Code for our experiments is available at https://github.com/ch-engpan/IL_imperfect.

4.1 Environment and datasets

We evaluate our algorithm against baseline methods on four MuJoCo environments Todorov et al. (2012); Towers et al. (2024) and conduct ablation studies to assess the contributions of our proposed components. Demonstrations are collected by training a policy with SAC with the true reward. An early-stage checkpoint πsub\pi^{\text{sub}} provides suboptimal demonstrations, while the final checkpoint π∗\pi^{*} provides optimal demonstrations (see Appendix Table 71 for the checkpoints’ performance). As in Beliaev et al. (2022); Tangkaratt et al. (2020), the imperfect dataset is mixture of state-action pairs from π∗\pi^{*} and πsub\pi^{\text{sub}}. Unlike random behaviors, our suboptimal data comes from a real suboptimal policy, which reflects that experts may make mistakes, but their actions are still better than random actions. Using this approach, multiple imperfect demonstration sets D={(i,Di)}i=1mD=\{(i,D_{i})\}^{m}_{i=1} are collected.

4.2 Comparison with Baselines

Across the experiments, we benchmark our model against four IL baseline algorithms. (1) GAIL o.s. (optimal subset) Ho and Ermon (2016): GAIL trained on the purely optimal subset of demonstrations, serving as an oracle method; (2) GAIL: GAIL trained on all (optimal and suboptimal) demonstrations; (3) RIL Tangkaratt et al. (2020): trains an optimality discriminator via pseudo-labeling with co-training; (4) WGAIL Wang et al. (2021): estimates importance weights to emphasize near-optimal demonstrations; (5) ILEED Beliaev et al. (2022): learns the policy in a offline training manner via maximum-likelihood; (6) BC Pomerleau (1988). For fair comparison, we adopt a consistent model architecture for discriminator/classifier/scoring model, and learner policy, modifying only the input and output layers to match the state and action spaces of each environment Arulkumaran and Lillrank (2024). Moreover, all online baselines incorporate mixup regularization. All learner policies are updated using SAC with same hyperparameters. Training details are provided in Appendix Table 7.2. We use 5 random seeds per condition and report the mean and standard deviation in all our results. For offline methods (ILEED and BC), for each random seed, we repeat the algorithm 10 times with random initializations and report the best result by selecting the run with the maximal likelihood.

The results are summarized in Table 2 (see Appendix Fig. 72 for training curves, and Supplementary Table S8 for more detailed results of offline methods). In the general expertise test, our algorithm outperforms all baselines except GAIL o.s., achieving at least twice the rewards in all tasks. While GAIL o.s. attains comparable rewards, our algorithm still yields slightly higher rewards in Ant, Swimmer and Walker2d. This is attributed to the fact that our algorithm can achieve high classification performance on imperfect demonstrations (see Table 4), and, in contrast to GAIL o.s., is also capable of leveraging suboptimal data to perform better in the subsequent online IL stage. In the low expertise test, the trends remain similar: our algorithm surpasses all baselines except GAIL o.s. However, decreased classification performance on imperfect demonstrations (see Table 4) reduces overall rewards compared to the general expertise test. In this setting, GAIL o.s., which trains on purely optimal subset of demonstrations, achieves higher rewards in most tasks.

The low rewards achieved by other baselines in both experiments can be attributed to the several factors. For GAIL, which treats all demonstrations as optimal, its performance is limited when handling imperfect demonstrations. RIL assumes that most demonstrations are optimal, but in our experiments, at least half are suboptimal. Consequently, the discriminator’s classification risk does not align with the risk of distinguishing between optimal and suboptimal demonstrations, reducing the reliability of its predictions for policy learning. Moreover, even with co-training for pseudo-labeling, the overconfidence can only be partially mitigated; once error accumulation begins, it continues to degrade the discriminator’s ability to predict optimality of demonstrations. WGAIL requires an optimal discriminator to compute importance weights, assuming the early-stage GAIL discriminator is near-optimal. Although early stopping is used for weight estimation, this assumption can fail due to the instability of adversarial learning. ILEED is sensitive to state embedding quality and assumes uniform state coverage, making it prone to biased expertise estimates under sparse data. Being offline and MLE-based, it is vulnerable to distribution shift, and its tightly coupled joint optimization can lead to instability.

4.3 Estimation of expertise levels

Table 3 reports the estimation errors of the scoring model trained in Stage 1 w.r.t. expertise levels relative to the ground truth, with detailed results provided in Appendix Tables 73-74. In the general expertise test, where true expertise levels are widely distributed within [0.1-0.9], errors are extremely low, remaining below 0.004 across all tasks. In contrast, in the low expertise test, with levels [0.05-0.15], the estimation errors increase to around 0.1 for most tasks. This indicates that the scoring model tends to be over-optimistic and produce more false positive (FP) labels on imperfect demonstrations (see Appendix Table 74). However, these incorrect labels are largely corrected during Stage 2.

4.4 Optimality Prediction on Imperfection Demonstrations

We evaluate the scoring model fϕf_{\phi} on its ability to classify imperfect demonstrations by optimality. Labeling is performed in two stages: Stage 1 uses pretrained fϕf_{\phi} and Stage 2 uses fine-tuned fϕf_{\phi}. Performance is measured using accuracy and precision, with a focus on precision, as it reflects the FP risk, which is more critical than false negative risk for policy learning Irpan et al. (2019).

Results in Table 4 show that in the general expertise test, both accuracy and precision are nearly 1 in Stage 1, leaving almost no room for improvement in Stage 2. In contrast, in the low expertise test, where expertise levels are narrowly distributed, the accuracy in Stage 1 stays above 86%, but the precision drops significantly, to 43-78%. This indicates that surrogate demonstrator classification training handles datasets with widely varying expertise well, but struggles when expertise levels are similar. However, Stage 2 improves both accuracy and precision, with precision increasing by 12-115% across tasks. This shows that for imperfect demonstrations with extremely low expertise, many false positives from a poorly pretrained fϕf_{\phi} can be corrected in Stage 2 after fine-tuning fϕf_{\phi}. Detailed classification results are presented in Appendix Table 74.

4.5 Ablation tests

To assess the effect of each component of our algorithm, we conduct ablation experiments on the Ant-v4 environment.

Relabeling and Early Stopping: We evaluate the effects of the relabeling step and early stopping in Stage 2 (Algorithm 2), shown in Fig. 2 (a)-(b) (see Appendix Table 75 for numerical results). Without relabeling, performance is comparable to the original method in the general expertise test but drops by about half in the low expertise test due to FP errors generated in Stage 1 (see Sec. 4.4), which cannot be corrected without Stage 2 relabeling. Removing early stopping degrades rewards in both general and low expertise tests as the agent approaches the optimal policy. Near-optimal agent samples confuse fϕf_{\phi}, increasing classification errors and accumulating incorrect labels, which reinforces overconfidence of fϕf_{\phi} and corrupts the surrogate reward for the agent.

Top-kk kk Value Selection: We study the effect of different kk values on IL performance . Results are shown in Fig. 2 (c)-(d) and Appendix Table 76. For both the general and low expertise tests, (average optimality ratios k∗=0.5k^{*}=0.5 and 0.10.1), rewards remain stable when k≤k∗k\leq k^{*} but decline for k>k∗k>k^{*}. The reason is that the pseudo-optimal set consists of the ⌊k⋅|D|⌋\lfloor k\cdot|D|\rfloor state–action pairs with the highest fϕf_{\phi} scores. Assuming fϕf_{\phi} is well trained, a k<k∗k<k^{*} leads to a conservative selection (subset of the true optimal set), while k>k∗k>k^{*} can introduce more FP samples to the pseudo optimal set. This indicates that FP risk is more critical, and a smaller kk is preferable.

Number of Demonstrators: We ablate the number of demonstrators and find that our method is robust to varying counts in terms of IL performance (see Supplementary Fig. S1 and Supplementary Tables S1–S2). Supplementary Sec. S2.2 and supplementary Fig. S3 show that our method consistently matches or outperforms variants (PN loss for discrimination, oracle settings with given expertise levels or optimality labels), highlighting its robustness and effectiveness.

Number of human queries: We analyze sensitivity to the number of human queries. Results (Supplementary Tables S3–S4 and Supplementary Fig. S4) show that even a single query performs comparably to five queries, due to the very high Stage 1 classification accuracy (>>99%) and similar reward performance across query settings. Nevertheless, queries remain necessary to assign correct labels to clusters in the absence of ground-truth annotations.

Expected Expertise α′\alpha^{\prime}: We analyze the effect of different values of α′\alpha^{\prime} (Supplementary Tables S5–S6 and Supplementary Fig. S5). Performance peaks near α′=0.5\alpha^{\prime}=0.5 and drops when α′\alpha^{\prime} is very small or large, indicating that α′=0.5\alpha^{\prime}=0.5 is optimal for both the general and low expertise tests.

5 Conclusions

We presented a general IL framework for handling unlabeled demonstrations from heterogeneous imperfect demonstrators with unknown expertise. Our approach combines EM-style alternating self-training with an online refinement step to learn a scoring model that guides policy learning. Experiments across challenging settings demonstrate strong performance, especially in low-expertise regimes, highlighting the value of our method’s ability to leverage suboptimal data in an (almost) unsupervised manner.

Supplementary Information
Imitating the Imperfect: Offline-to-Online Robust Imitation Learning from Heterogeneous Demonstrators
This document provides further discussion of related work, detailed experimental and ablation results, additional analysis of method variants, and reproducibility details for the accompanying article.

Supplementary Sec. S1 Further Discussion on Related Work

Closer comparisons with ILEED Beliaev et al. (2022)

ILEED is the closest work to ours, as both address IL from multiple demonstrators with heterogeneous expertise. Despite the shared high-level motivation, the two approaches differ substantially in problem setting, modeling assumptions, methodologies and robustness properties, making them suitable for different practical regimes.

  • •

    Problem setting. ILEED considers the problem setting where each demonstrator’s policy is a mixture of the optimal policy and a uniformly random policy, with the mixing coefficient interpreted as an expertise level.11 1 For continuous action spaces, ILEED replaces this uniform noise component with a high-entropy variant of the optimal policy. Specifically, the suboptimal component is modeled by scaling the variance of a Gaussian mixture policy, resulting in a near-uniform distribution rather than a structured suboptimal policy. While convenient, this “suboptimal = uniform noise” assumption is restrictive as real-world suboptimal behavior is typically structured, rather than near-uniform noise. For example, a demonstrator may consistently struggle with specific skills without acting randomly overall.

    In contrast, we relax this assumption by modeling each demonstrator’s behavior as a mixture of the optimal policy and an unknown suboptimal policy. Our formulation imposes no uniformity or high-entropy constraints on the suboptimal component, enabling the method to capture realistic and highly structured forms of suboptimality.

  • •

    Expertise modeling. ILEED models expertise as a state-dependent function defined as a sigmoid of the inner product between the learned state and demonstrator embeddings. Although this formulation can represent state-varying expertise, it relies heavily on the quality of the recovered embeddings for all states visited by all demonstrators. In practice, when demonstrators explore only partial or disjoint regions of the state space, the resulting embeddings, and thus the inferred expertise levels, can become severely biased, causing significant policy degradation.

    Our method instead models expertise through the class-prior probability ℙ⁡(z=1)\mathbb{P}(z{=}1), estimated via a surrogate scoring model that directly distinguishes optimal from suboptimal samples across demonstrators. This approach does not require each demonstrator to provide full coverage of the state space. Moreover, the trained scoring model outputs the sample-wise optimality probability fϕ​(s,a)=ℙ⁡(z=1∣s,a)f_{\phi}(s,a)=\mathbb{P}(z{=}1\mid s,a), and we use the surrogate reward rϕ​(s,a)=−log⁡(1−fϕ​(s,a))r_{\phi}(s,a)=-\log(1-f_{\phi}(s,a)) to train the RL agent (SAC).

  • •

    Methodology. ILEED performs fully offline maximum-likelihood estimation of the policy, state embeddings, and demonstrator embeddings. As a result, it is sensitive to distribution shift between the demonstration distribution and the agent’s on-policy distribution during training.

    Our method instead employs a two-stage procedure: we first learn a scoring model offline, use the surrogate reward rϕ​(s,a)=−log⁡(1−fϕ​(s,a))r_{\phi}(s,a)=-\log(1-f_{\phi}(s,a)) to train an RL agent, and iteratively refine the scorer using on-policy rollouts. To explicitly mitigate covariate shift, we incorporate mixup augmentation, an agent-matching penalty, and a relabeling mechanism, making our approach more robust when the agent visits states that rarely or never appear in the demonstrations.

  • •

    Optimization stability. ILEED jointly optimizes policy parameters, state embeddings, and demonstrator embeddings via a single maximum-likelihood objective. This fully coupled optimization can be unstable, as conflicting gradients among latent components may lead to degenerate solutions.

    Our method instead employs an EM-style alternating self-training method that alternates between surrogate-risk minimization for the scoring model and expertise estimation from the current hard pseudo-labels. Policy learning then proceeds through a standard RL pipeline using the scoring model as a reward proxy, yielding an empirically effective optimization procedure.

Our empirical results (see Table 2 and Appendix Fig. 72 in the main article, and Supplementary Table S8) validate these distinctions. In particular, our method is advantageous when demonstrations contain structured suboptimality, exhibit low expertise levels, or when distribution shift between demonstrations and agent rollouts is significant.

Comparisons with T‑REX/D‑REX Brown et al. (2019); Brown et al. (2020)

Both trajectory-ranked reward extrapolation (T-REX) and disturbance-based reward extrapolation (D-REX) learn a reward function from ranked demonstrations, allowing an agent to potentially outperform the demonstrator via extrapolation. T-REX relies on experts to provide ranking comparisons, while D-REX can automatically generate rankings by injecting noise into a cloned policy, based on the assumption that added noise leads to a continuous degradation in performance.

Compared to T-REX, our method does not require large amounts of supervision or expert ranking feedback during training. Moreover, while D-REX assumes homogeneous demonstrations and introduces heterogeneity artificially, our approach naturally handles heterogeneous datasets and is capable of inferring varying expertise levels within the data. Unlike D-REX, our method does not rely on the assumption that policy performance monotonically decreases with noise injection, which may not hold in more complex domains. In addition, both T-REX and D-REX first learn a surrogate reward function and then optimize a policy using RL on this fixed reward, which can lead to covariate shift when the agent encounters states not present in the demonstrations. Our method addresses this issue by continuously fine-tuning the scoring model with new data collected during RL, resulting in improved robustness and generalization. Overall, our approach provides a flexible and practical framework for leveraging demonstrations, particularly in settings with heterogeneous data and limited supervision.

Comparisons with VPIL Cai et al. (2023)

Vaguely pairwise imitation learning (VPIL) investigates a weak-supervision setting in which the annotator provides vague pairwise feedback: a pair of demonstrations is labeled only when their quality differs substantially, resulting in two contaminated datasets that still contain mixtures of expert and non-expert trajectories. VPIL leverages this pairwise structure to recover the expert occupancy measure through mixture-proportion estimation (Ramaswamy et al., 2016, MPE;) and risk rewriting, and its comparative imitation learning with risk rewriting with estimation (COMPILER-E) algorithms integrate the recovered distribution into a GAIL-style adversarial IL framework.

Our problem setting is more general and arguably more challenging. Unlike VPIL, which assumes access to vague pairwise comparison labels, we consider a scenario in which the agent receives only heterogeneous demonstrations of unknown and varying quality, with no preference, ranking, or optimality labels. In the absence of such supervision, the learner must infer both the underlying demonstration quality and the reward surrogate directly from unlabeled trajectories.

The methodological differences therefore extend beyond supervision assumptions. Rather than reconstructing an expert occupancy measure from pairwise datasets, we learn a fine-grained state–action optimality scoring model through a surrogate demonstrator classification objective and an EM-style alternating self-training procedure for latent expertise estimation. The trained scoring model then serves as a surrogate reward within an iterative policy-learning loop, enabling robust imitation learning directly from heterogeneous, unlabeled demonstrators without relying on any preference-based supervision.

Comparisons with AIRL Fu et al. (2017)

Adversarial inverse reinforcement learning (AIRL) extends the GAIL framework by structuring the discriminator to decompose into a state-only reward term and a shaping term, enabling recovery of a reward function that is disentangled from environment dynamics. This structure allows AIRL to learn portable rewards that can be re-optimized in new or modified environments.

Our problem setting, however, is fundamentally different. Rather than assuming demonstrations come from a single (near-optimal) expert, we address imitation learning from heterogeneous, unlabeled, and potentially highly suboptimal demonstrators with unknown expertise levels. Although our method learns a scoring model that serves as a surrogate reward, the objective is not reward recovery or transfer, but robust policy learning when expert dominance does not hold. AIRL, like GAIL, is not designed to handle heterogeneous demonstrators and presumes access to expert demonstrations. Therefore, their assumptions and objectives cannot address the key challenges in our setting.

Supplementary Sec. S2 Experiment Details

S2.1 Detailed results & Ablation studies

Number of Demonstrators: The results in Supplementary Table S1 show that the estimation error of expertise levels in low expertise test increase when the number of demonstrators is reduced. However, the reward obtained by the IL agent in Stage 2 (see Supplementary Table S2) does not decrease substantially. These results demonstrate the robustness of our method with respect to varying demonstrator counts in terms of IL performance.

Number of Human Queries: To study the sensitivity to the number of human queries, we conducted ablation experiments, varying the number of queries. The results are shown in Supplementary Tables S3–S4 and Supplementary Fig. S4. We observe that even with only a single query, our method still achieves similar performance to that obtained with 5 queries. This is because the classification accuracy in Stage 1 is extremely high (above 99%), making it very unlikely for the system to select an incorrectly labeled sample that would lead to completely opposite or flipped classification results. Also, the learned policies across different numbers of queries have similar performance in final reward achieved.

Then, we explain the necessity of this query. In our problem setting, we do not have labels for either sample optimality or expertise levels. Without any labels, our classification method effectively performs an operation similar to clustering on the unlabeled data. A limited number of human queries is then used to ensure that the resulting clusters are assigned the correct labels. We select 5 as the number of queries so that the procedure remains both effective and practical.

Expected Expertise α′\alpha^{\prime}: To study the sensitivity to the value of α′\alpha^{\prime}, we conduct ablation studies examining the effect of different α′\alpha^{\prime} values. Supplementary Table S5 presents the classification results of the scoring model, while Supplementary Table S6 and Supplementary Fig. S5 report the rewards obtained by the learned policies. The performance of both the scoring model and the learned policy is maximized when α′\alpha^{\prime} is close to 0.5, and degrades when α′\alpha^{\prime} is extremely small or large. These results indicate that selecting α′=0.5\alpha^{\prime}=0.5 yields the best performance for both the general expertise and low expertise test settings.

Number of Initializations for Scoring Model Training: We report the number of initializations required by Algorithm 1 in the main article in Supplementary Table S7. For the general expertise test, we use a single initialization until the Expertise Dispersion Criterion is satisfied. In more challenging low expertise cases, the number of initializations increases but remains fewer than 10. These results demonstrate that our algorithm is computationally efficient in practice.

S2.2 Additional Analysis of Method Variants

We analyze our algorithm by comparing it against several variants under different settings. (1) Scoring: original method; (2) Scoring PN: in Stage 2, the first term 𝔼^(s,a)∼ρ​[ℓ⁡(T⁡(fϕ​(s,a)),z¯)]\widehat{\mathbb{E}}_{(s,a)\sim\rho}\big[\ell(T(f_{\phi}(s,a)),\bar{z})\big] (demonstration discriminative loss) in Eq. 5 of the main article is replaced with a positive-negative (PN) classification loss (binary cross-entropy) 𝔼^(s,a)∼ρ^π∗(s′,a′)∼ρ^πsub​[ℒPN​(fϕ​(s,a),fϕ​(s′,a′))]\widehat{\mathbb{E}}_{\begin{subarray}{c}(s,a)\sim\hat{\rho}^{\pi^{*}}\\ (s^{\prime},a^{\prime})\sim\hat{\rho}^{\pi^{\mathrm{sub}}}\end{subarray}}\big[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PN}}(f_{\phi}(s,a),f_{\phi}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime}))\big], where ℒPN​(fϕ​(s,a),fϕ​(s′,a′))=−log⁡fϕ​(s,a)−log⁡(1−fϕ​(s′,a′))\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PN}}(f_{\phi}(s,a),f_{\phi}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime}))=-\log f_{\phi}(s,a)-\log(1-f_{\phi}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})). Here, ρ^π∗\hat{\rho}^{\pi^{*}} and ρ^πsub\hat{\rho}^{\pi^{\mathrm{sub}}} represent the pseudo-optimal and pseudo-suboptimal data distributions inferred from DoptD_{\mathrm{opt}} and Dsubopt=D∖DoptD_{\mathrm{subopt}}=D\setminus D_{\mathrm{opt}}, respectively. Thus, pseudo-optimal samples have target 1 and pseudo-suboptimal samples have target 0, consistent with the released binary-cross-entropy implementation. (3) Scoring exp. known: the true expertise levels are assumed to be given in both Stage 1 and 2. (4) Scoring opt. known: in Stage 2, DoptD_{\mathrm{opt}} is provided based on the true labels.

The results in Supplementary Fig. S3 show that, overall, all methods achieve comparable performance. Scoring PN yields slightly lower rewards in general expertise test on Ant and Swimmer tasks, which may be attributed to the overconfidence issue introduced by self-labeling when using the PN loss. This result highlights the effectiveness of our demonstration discriminative loss. Scoring exp. known and Scoring opt. known serve as oracle variants (with oracle knowledge of expertise levels and optimality labels, respectively) and achieve only marginally better performance than the original method in the low expertise test on HalfCheetah and Walker2d. This observation highlights the effectiveness of our approach in expertise-level estimation and optimality prediction when learning from imperfect demonstrations.
